text: Given the heights of a histogram, where each bar has width one, return the area of the largest rectangle you can form.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a rectangle at some bar's height can extend left and right only while the bars stay at least that tall; it stops at the first shorter bar on each side. So each bar needs its nearest shorter bar on both sides. Right?
Exactly. Up to ten to the fifth bars, and each height is at most ten to the fourth.
Got it. So the real task is finding the nearest shorter bar on both sides of every bar — and with up to a hundred thousand bars, I want to do it in one pass.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach expands from each bar to find its shorter boundaries — that's quadratic, too slow for a hundred thousand bars. This problem reminds me of a monotonic stack, because it finds every nearest-smaller boundary in linear time. Increasing or decreasing? The rule I use: the stack holds elements still waiting for a boundary, and an element is popped exactly when the incoming one is its boundary. I want the nearest smaller, so I pop whenever the incoming bar is less than or equal to the top — which keeps the stack increasing. If I were looking for the nearest greater instead, it would be a decreasing stack.

Here's the plan. One: keep an increasing stack of indices, and append a negative-one sentinel to the heights. Two: for each index, while the top bar is at least as tall as the current one, pop it and settle its rectangle. Three: push the current index. One thing worth flagging — when I pop a bar, its right boundary is the current i, and its left boundary is whatever sits below it now, so the width is the open interval, i minus top minus one. And the trailing negative-one sentinel is shorter than every bar, so it flushes any bars still left on the stack at the end. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I append the sentinel, then walk every index. While the top of the stack is at least as tall as the current bar, I pop it, compute its width, and update the max area with height times width. Then I push the current index. One thing worth flagging — if the stack is empty after popping, there's no shorter bar to the left, so the width runs all the way to the start: w equals i. Otherwise it's i minus the new top minus one. And height times width peaks at ten to the fourth times ten to the fifth, which is ten to the ninth — still within int.

Let's dry-run the code on two, one, five, six, two, three, with the sentinel appended. Expected ten. The row that matters is i equals four, height two. It pops bar three for six by one, then bar two, height five: its left boundary is index one and its right is four, so the width is two and the area is ten. Notice that one step pops two bars — each bar is popped only once overall, which is why it's linear. The sentinel flushes the rest, and nothing beats ten. That matches. Corner cases: a strictly increasing histogram is flushed entirely by the sentinel. A single bar returns its own height. With equal heights, the rightmost equal bar gets the full width.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is linear — each bar is pushed and popped at most once, so the inner while loop is amortized. The space complexity is linear for the stack. Oh, one more thing — this is a reusable engine. For the largest rectangle of ones in a binary matrix, I'd build a histogram per row and run this on each row.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You picked an increasing stack from the rule: nearest smaller means increasing. You nailed the open-interval width and the empty-stack case. And you used the sentinel to flush cleanly, then connected it to the binary-matrix version. Good work.
